claims.text: The initial material is homogeneous Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase stability of the high-temperature BCC state is governed by a threshold in Al diffusivity.
A critical dwell time within 1100–800 °C permits transformation of the high-temperature BCC state.
Within the intermediate-temperature regime, Al diffuses significantly faster than Cr, Co, Fe, and Ni.
Enhanced Al mobility causes local Al accumulation and formation of Al-rich clusters.
Differential diffusion produces localized chemical short-range ordering.
Al-rich clustering destabilizes the high-temperature BCC configuration through a composition-driven thermodynamic instability.
The composition-driven instability triggers secondary-phase nucleation.
Longer dwell times in the intermediate-temperature range will increase the volume fraction of secondary phases.
Secondary-phase formation will produce new diffraction peaks whose intensities increase with dwell time.
AIMD will reveal a temperature or time threshold at which Al diffusivity sharply increases relative to that of the other elements.
Rapid quenching minimizes the time available for Al diffusion.
Rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state yields minimal secondary-phase formation.
The proposed mechanism applies within 1100–800 °C under a controlled inert atmosphere.
Under rapid cooling or at temperatures outside the stated window, other diffusion or transformation mechanisms may dominate.
Failure to observe both the predicted Al-diffusivity crossover and the associated increase in secondary-phase formation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
